Plaque "Sakattsura Isosaki Shrine" written by [[Prince Komatsu Akihito]]]] '''Sakattsura Isosaki Shrine''' (さかつらいそさきじんじゃ) is a [[Shinto shrine]] located in [[Hitachinaka City]], [[Ibaraki Prefecture]]. It is classified as a [[Myōjin Taisha|Myōjin Taisha]] under the [[Engishiki|Engishiki system]]. The former shrine Rank was [[National Middle Shrine|Kokuhei Chūsha]], and it is now a [[Beppyo Shrine]] under the [[Association of Shinto Shrines]]. == Overview == The shrine is situated on a hill facing the [[Pacific Ocean]] in eastern [[Ibaraki Prefecture]]. It is closely related to [[Ōarai Isosaki Shrine]] in [[Ōarai Town]] across the [[Naka River]], and the two shrines form a single faith. == Deities == '''Main deity''' * '''[[Sukunahikona no Mikoto]]''' (少彦名命) *: Known for helping [[Ōkuninushi|Ōnamuchi no Mikoto]] (Ōkuninushi no Mikoto) in creating the land. '''Enshrined deity''' * [[Ōkuninushi|Ōnamuchi no Mikoto]] (大名持命) *: Another name for [[Ōkuninushi no Mikoto]] (大己貴命), the deity of [[Ōarai Isosaki Shrine]], and his divided spirit. He is said to have created the land with the help of Sukunahikona no Mikoto. In the myths found in the [[Kojiki]], [[Nihon Shoki]], and [[Fudoki]], these two deities often appear together in the stories of land creation. Many shrines enshrine this combination of deities. At this shrine, Sukunahikona no Mikoto is also considered [[Ebisu]] of the [[Seven Lucky Gods]], and Ōnamuchi no Mikoto is considered [[Daikokuten]]. == History == === Founding === According to the [[Nihon Montoku Tennō Jitsuroku]], a deity appeared at Ōarai Isosaki in [[Kashima District, Hitachi Province]] in Saikō 3rd year (856). {{quotation| Hitachi Province reports that a new deity has descended at Ōarai Isosaki in Kashima District. Initially, a salt maker saw a shining light in the sea at midnight. The next day, two strange stones appeared on the shore, each about a foot high. The following day, more than twenty small stones appeared around the strange stones, resembling attendants. The stones were vividly colored and shaped like monks, but without ears or eyes. The divine spirit possessed a person and said, "I am Ōnamuchi and Sukunahikona. We finished creating this land and went to the eastern sea, but we have returned to save the people." |Nihon Montoku Tennō Jitsuroku, Saikō 3rd year, December戊戌条}} Thus, Ōkuninushi no Mikoto (Ōnamuchi) was enshrined at Ōarai, and Sukunahikona no Mikoto was enshrined at Sakattsura, marking the founding of the two shrines. The rock formations along the coast near the shrine are tilted about 45 degrees to the south, and the part that tilts to the north is called "Gyaku-retsu" (逆列, Reverse Row), which is said to be the origin of the shrine's name. Later, it came to be known as "Sakattsura" because it enshrined the god of sake (alcohol)[http://www.oyashiro.or.jp/link/0006.html Sakattsura Isosaki Shrine] (Ibaraki Prefecture Shrine Office). === Historical Overview === The [[Engishiki]] lists the shrine as "Hitachi Province Naka District Sakattsura Isosaki Yakushi Bosatsu Shrine" and classifies it as a Myōjin Taisha. The shrine fell into decline during the [[Middle Ages]] and lost its buildings. In the [[Early Modern Period]], the second lord of the [[Mito Domain]], [[Tokugawa Mitsukuni]], initiated the rebuilding of the shrine, and the third lord, [[Tokugawa Tsunaeda]], relocated and restored it to its current location. The old site is said to be near the first torii. In 1885 (Meiji 18), the shrine was Ranked as a [[National Middle Shrine|Kokuhei Chūsha]] under the [[Modern Shrine Rank System]]. It is now officially named "Sakattsura Isosaki Shrine." === Shrine Rankings === * [[Ten'an]] 1st year (857), August 7 - Received official shrine status (Nihon Montoku Tennō Jitsuroku) * Ten'an 1st year (857), October 15 - Granted the title "Yakushi Bosatsu Myōjin" (Nihon Montoku Tennō Jitsuroku) == Grounds == The carving of a squirrel and grapes on the front of the haiden is said to be the work of [[Hidari Jingorō]]. The guardian dogs (komainu) on either side of the second torii were made by a Showa period stone mason named Heikichi Iizuka. The path to the shrine is lined with camellia, tabunoki, and sudajii trees, forming a broadleaf forest that is designated a Natural Monument by Ibaraki Prefecture. The original shrine site is believed to be near the first torii, around the ruins of Hikantei. Plaque "Sakattsura Isosaki Shrine" written by [[Prince Komatsu Akihito]]]] '''Sakattsura Isosaki Shrine''' (さかつらいそさきじんじゃ) is a [[Shinto shrine]] located in [[Hitachinaka City]], [[Ibaraki Prefecture]]. It is classified as a [[Myōjin Taisha|Myōjin Taisha]] under the [[Engishiki|Engishiki system]]. The former shrine Rank was [[National Middle Shrine|Kokuhei Chūsha]], and it is now a [[Beppyo Shrine]] under the [[Association of Shinto Shrines]]. == Overview == The shrine is situated on a hill facing the [[Pacific Ocean]] in eastern [[Ibaraki Prefecture]]. It is closely related to [[Ōarai Isosaki Shrine]] in [[Ōarai Town]] across the [[Naka River]], and the two shrines form a single faith. == Deities == '''Main deity''' * '''[[Sukunahikona no Mikoto]]''' (少彦名命) *: Known for helping [[Ōkuninushi|Ōnamuchi no Mikoto]] (Ōkuninushi no Mikoto) in creating the land. '''Enshrined deity''' * [[Ōkuninushi|Ōnamuchi no Mikoto]] (大名持命) *: Another name for [[Ōkuninushi no Mikoto]] (大己貴命), the deity of [[Ōarai Isosaki Shrine]], and his divided spirit. He is said to have created the land with the help of Sukunahikona no Mikoto. In the myths found in the [[Kojiki]], [[Nihon Shoki]], and [[Fudoki]], these two deities often appear together in the stories of land creation. Many shrines enshrine this combination of deities. At this shrine, Sukunahikona no Mikoto is also considered [[Ebisu]] of the [[Seven Lucky Gods]], and Ōnamuchi no Mikoto is considered [[Daikokuten]]. == History == === Founding === According to the [[Nihon Montoku Tennō Jitsuroku]], a deity appeared at Ōarai Isosaki in [[Kashima District, Hitachi Province]] in Saikō 3rd year (856). {{quotation| Hitachi Province reports that a new deity has descended at Ōarai Isosaki in Kashima District. Initially, a salt maker saw a shining light in the sea at midnight. The next day, two strange stones appeared on the shore, each about a foot high. The following day, more than twenty small stones appeared around the strange stones, resembling attendants. The stones were vividly colored and shaped like monks, but without ears or eyes. The divine spirit possessed a person and said, "I am Ōnamuchi and Sukunahikona. We finished creating this land and went to the eastern sea, but we have returned to save the people." |Nihon Montoku Tennō Jitsuroku, Saikō 3rd year, December戊戌条}} Thus, Ōkuninushi no Mikoto (Ōnamuchi) was enshrined at Ōarai, and Sukunahikona no Mikoto was enshrined at Sakattsura, marking the founding of the two shrines. The rock formations along the coast near the shrine are tilted about 45 degrees to the south, and the part that tilts to the north is called "Gyaku-retsu" (逆列, Reverse Row), which is said to be the origin of the shrine's name. Later, it came to be known as "Sakattsura" because it enshrined the god of sake (alcohol)[http://www.oyashiro.or.jp/link/0006.html Sakattsura Isosaki Shrine] (Ibaraki Prefecture Shrine Office). === Historical Overview === The [[Engishiki]] lists the shrine as "Hitachi Province Naka District Sakattsura Isosaki Yakushi Bosatsu Shrine" and classifies it as a Myōjin Taisha. The shrine fell into decline during the [[Middle Ages]] and lost its buildings. In the [[Early Modern Period]], the second lord of the [[Mito Domain]], [[Tokugawa Mitsukuni]], initiated the rebuilding of the shrine, and the third lord, [[Tokugawa Tsunaeda]], relocated and restored it to its current location. The old site is said to be near the first torii. In 1885 (Meiji 18), the shrine was Ranked as a [[National Middle Shrine|Kokuhei Chūsha]] under the [[Modern Shrine Rank System]]. It is now officially named "Sakattsura Isosaki Shrine." === Shrine Rankings === * [[Ten'an]] 1st year (857), August 7 - Received official shrine status (Nihon Montoku Tennō Jitsuroku) * Ten'an 1st year (857), October 15 - Granted the title "Yakushi Bosatsu Myōjin" (Nihon Montoku Tennō Jitsuroku) == Grounds == The carving of a squirrel and grapes on the front of the haiden is said to be the work of [[Hidari Jingorō]]. The guardian dogs (komainu) on either side of the second torii were made by a Showa period stone mason named Heikichi Iizuka. The path to the shrine is lined with camellia, tabunoki, and sudajii trees, forming a broadleaf forest that is designated a Natural Monument by Ibaraki Prefecture. The original shrine site is believed to be near the first torii, around the ruins of Hikantei. File:Sakattsura Isosaki Shrine main hall.JPG|main hall File:Sakattsura Isosaki Shrine Worship Hall.JPG|Worship Hall File:Sakattsura Isosaki Shrine Stone where Tokugawa Nariaki sat.JPG|Stone where [[Tokugawa Nariaki]] sat File:Sakattsura Isosaki Shrine Second Torii.JPG|Second Torii File:Sakattsura Isosaki Shrine Approach.JPG|Approach (Prefectural Natural Monument) == Auxiliary Shrines == [[File:Sakattsura Chinjusha (Auxiliary Shrine of Sakattsura Isosaki Shrine).JPG|thumb|200px|Sakattsura Chinjusha]] [[File:Sakattsura Isosaki Shrine Auxiliary Shrines.JPG|thumb|200px|Five Auxiliary Shrines]] * Sakattsura Chinjusha (さかつらちんれいしゃ) ** Enshrined deity: 506 war dead from the [[Russo-Japanese War]] to [[World War II]] *: Located north of the main hall. * Inari Shrine - Enshrined deity: [[Ukanomitama|Ukanomitama no Mikoto]] * Tenmangū - Enshrined deity: [[Sugawara no Michizane]] * Kotohira Shrine - Enshrined deity: [[Ōmononushi|Ōmononushi no Mikoto]] * Fuji Shrine - Enshrined deity: [[Konohanasakuya-hime]], worshipped as a deity of safe childbirth. * Water Shrine - Enshrined deity: [[Mizuhanome|Mizuhanome no Mikoto]] == Cultural Properties == === Ibaraki Prefecture Designated Natural Monument === * Sakattsura Isosaki Shrine Tree Grove - The broadleaf forest of camellia, tabunoki, and sudajii trees along the approach and surrounding the grounds. Designated in 2005. == location Information == '''location''' * [[Ibaraki Prefecture]], [[Hitachinaka City]], Isosaki Town 4607-2 '''Transportation Access''' * Nearest station: [[Hitachinaka Seaside Railway]], [[Hitachinaka Seaside Railway Minato Line|Minato Line]], [[:en:Ajigaura Station|Ajigaura Station]] (about 15 minutes on foot) - The terminal station of the Minato Line. '''Nearby''' * Ruins of Hikantei - Ruins of a pavilion built by the Mito Domain. Designated a Historic Site by Hitachinaka City. * Kanto Place - A scenic spot selected by the lords of the Mito Domain. Designated a Scenic Spot by Hitachinaka City. * Kawagozuka Kofun - Designated a Historic Site by Hitachinaka City. * Hiraiso Cretaceous Layer - Nearby coast. Designated a Natural Monument by Ibaraki Prefecture. == References == {{reflist}} == Related Books == * Anzu Moto, Umeda Yoshihiko, editors and supervisors, "Shinto Dictionary", [[Shinto Shinpōsha]], It is closely related to [[Ōarai Isosaki Shrine]] in [[Ōarai Town]] across the [[Naka River]], and the two shrines form a single faith. == Deities == '''Main deity''' * '''[[Sukunahikona no Mikoto]]''' (少彦名命) *: Known for helping [[Ōkuninushi|Ōnamuchi no Mikoto]] (Ōkuninushi no Mikoto) in creating the land. '''Enshrined deity''' * [[Ōkuninushi|Ōnamuchi no Mikoto]] (大名持命) *: Another name for [[Ōkuninushi no Mikoto]] (大己貴命), the deity of [[Ōarai Isosaki Shrine]], and his divided spirit. He is said to have created the land with the help of Sukunahikona no Mikoto. In the myths found in the [[Kojiki]], [[Nihon Shoki]], and [[Fudoki]], these two deities often appear together in the stories of land creation. Many shrines enshrine this combination of deities. At this shrine, Sukunahikona no Mikoto is also considered [[Ebisu]] of the [[Seven Lucky Gods]], and Ōnamuchi no Mikoto is considered [[Daikokuten]]. == History == === Founding === According to the [[Nihon Montoku Tennō Jitsuroku]], a deity appeared at Ōarai Isosaki in [[Kashima District, Hitachi Province]] in Saikō 3rd year (856). {{quotation| Hitachi Province reports that a new deity has descended at Ōarai Isosaki in Kashima District. Initially, a salt maker saw a shining light in the sea at midnight. The next day, two strange stones appeared on the shore, each about a foot high. The following day, more than twenty small stones appeared around the strange stones, resembling attendants. The stones were vividly colored and shaped like monks, but without ears or eyes. The divine spirit possessed a person and said, "I am Ōnamuchi and Sukunahikona. We finished creating this land and went to the eastern sea, but we have returned to save the people." |Nihon Montoku Tennō Jitsuroku, Saikō 3rd year, December戊戌条}} Thus, Ōkuninushi no Mikoto (Ōnamuchi) was enshrined at Ōarai, and Sukunahikona no Mikoto was enshrined at Sakattsura, marking the founding of the two shrines. The rock formations along the coast near the shrine are tilted about 45 degrees to the south, and the part that tilts to the north is called "Gyaku-retsu" (逆列, Reverse Row), which is said to be the origin of the shrine's name. Later, it came to be known as "Sakattsura" because it enshrined the god of sake (alcohol)[http://www.oyashiro.or.jp/link/0006.html Sakattsura Isosaki Shrine] (Ibaraki Prefecture Shrine Office). === Historical Overview === The [[Engishiki]] lists the shrine as "Hitachi Province Naka District Sakattsura Isosaki Yakushi Bosatsu Shrine" and classifies it as a Myōjin Taisha. The shrine fell into decline during the [[Middle Ages]] and lost its buildings. In the [[Early Modern Period]], the second lord of the [[Mito Domain]], [[Tokugawa Mitsukuni]], initiated the rebuilding of the shrine, and the third lord, [[Tokugawa Tsunaeda]], relocated and restored it to its current location. The old site is said to be near the first torii. In 1885 (Meiji 18), the shrine was Ranked as a [[National Middle Shrine|Kokuhei Chūsha]] under the [[Modern Shrine Rank System]]. It is now officially named "Sakattsura Isosaki Shrine." === Shrine Rankings === * [[Ten'an]] 1st year (857), August 7 - Received official shrine status (Nihon Montoku Tennō Jitsuroku) * Ten'an 1st year (857), October 15 - Granted the title "Yakushi Bosatsu Myōjin" (Nihon Montoku Tennō Jitsuroku) == Grounds == The carving of a squirrel and grapes on the front of the haiden is said to be the work of [[Hidari Jingorō]]. The guardian dogs (komainu) on either side of the second torii were made by a Showa period stone mason named Heikichi Iizuka. The path to the shrine is lined with camellia, tabunoki, and sudajii trees, forming a broadleaf forest that is designated a Natural Monument by Ibaraki Prefecture. The original shrine site is believed to be near the first torii, around the ruins of Hikantei. Plaque "Sakattsura Isosaki Shrine" written by [[Prince Komatsu Akihito]]]] '''Sakattsura Isosaki Shrine''' (さかつらいそさきじんじゃ) is a [[Shinto shrine]] located in [[Hitachinaka City]], [[Ibaraki Prefecture]]. It is classified as a [[Myōjin Taisha|Myōjin Taisha]] under the [[Engishiki|Engishiki system]]. The former shrine Rank was [[National Middle Shrine|Kokuhei Chūsha]], and it is now a [[Beppyo Shrine]] under the [[Association of Shinto Shrines]]. == Overview == The shrine is situated on a hill facing the [[Pacific Ocean]] in eastern [[Ibaraki Prefecture]]. It is closely related to [[Ōarai Isosaki Shrine]] in [[Ōarai Town]] across the [[Naka River]], and the two shrines form a single faith. == Deities == '''Main deity''' * '''[[Sukunahikona no Mikoto]]''' (少彦名命) *: Known for helping [[Ōkuninushi|Ōnamuchi no Mikoto]] (Ōkuninushi no Mikoto) in creating the land. '''Enshrined deity''' * [[Ōkuninushi|Ōnamuchi no Mikoto]] (大名持命) *: Another name for [[Ōkuninushi no Mikoto]] (大己貴命), the deity of [[Ōarai Isosaki Shrine]], and his divided spirit. He is said to have created the land with the help of Sukunahikona no Mikoto. In the myths found in the [[Kojiki]], [[Nihon Shoki]], and [[Fudoki]], these two deities often appear together in the stories of land creation. Many shrines enshrine this combination of deities. At this shrine, Sukunahikona no Mikoto is also considered [[Ebisu]] of the [[Seven Lucky Gods]], and Ōnamuchi no Mikoto is considered [[Daikokuten]]. == History == === Founding === According to the [[Nihon Montoku Tennō Jitsuroku]], a deity appeared at Ōarai Isosaki in [[Kashima District, Hitachi Province]] in Saikō 3rd year (856). {{quotation| Hitachi Province reports that a new deity has descended at Ōarai Isosaki in Kashima District. Initially, a salt maker saw a shining light in the sea at midnight. The next day, two strange stones appeared on the shore, each about a foot high. The following day, more than twenty small stones appeared around the strange stones, resembling attendants. The stones were vividly colored and shaped like monks, but without ears or eyes. The divine spirit possessed a person and said, "I am Ōnamuchi and Sukunahikona. We finished creating this land and went to the eastern sea, but we have returned to save the people." |Nihon Montoku Tennō Jitsuroku, Saikō 3rd year, December戊戌条}} Thus, Ōkuninushi no Mikoto (Ōnamuchi) was enshrined at Ōarai, and Sukunahikona no Mikoto was enshrined at Sakattsura, marking the founding of the two shrines. The rock formations along the coast near the shrine are tilted about 45 degrees to the south, and the part that tilts to the north is called "Gyaku-retsu" (逆列, Reverse Row), which is said to be the origin of the shrine's name. Later, it came to be known as "Sakattsura" because it enshrined the god of sake (alcohol)[http://www.oyashiro.or.jp/link/0006.html Sakattsura Isosaki Shrine] (Ibaraki Prefecture Shrine Office). === Historical Overview === The [[Engishiki]] lists the shrine as "Hitachi Province Naka District Sakattsura Isosaki Yakushi Bosatsu Shrine" and classifies it as a Myōjin Taisha. The shrine fell into decline during the [[Middle Ages]] and lost its buildings. In the [[Early Modern Period]], the second lord of the [[Mito Domain]], [[Tokugawa Mitsukuni]], initiated the rebuilding of the shrine, and the third lord, [[Tokugawa Tsunaeda]], relocated and restored it to its current location. The old site is said to be near the first torii. In 1885 (Meiji 18), the shrine was Ranked as a [[National Middle Shrine|Kokuhei Chūsha]] under the [[Modern Shrine Rank System]]. It is now officially named "Sakattsura Isosaki Shrine." === Shrine Rankings === * [[Ten'an]] 1st year (857), August 7 - Received official shrine status (Nihon Montoku Tennō Jitsuroku) * Ten'an 1st year (857), October 15 - Granted the title "Yakushi Bosatsu Myōjin" (Nihon Montoku Tennō Jitsuroku) == Grounds == The carving of a squirrel and grapes on the front of the haiden is said to be the work of [[Hidari Jingorō]]. The guardian dogs (komainu) on either side of the second torii were made by a Showa period stone mason named Heikichi Iizuka. The path to the shrine is lined with camellia, tabunoki, and sudajii trees, forming a broadleaf forest that is designated a Natural Monument by Ibaraki Prefecture. The original shrine site is believed to be near the first torii, around the ruins of Hikantei. Designated in 2005. == location Information == '''location''' * [[Ibaraki Prefecture]], [[Hitachinaka City]], Isosaki Town 4607-2 '''Transportation Access''' * Nearest station: [[Hitachinaka Seaside Railway]], [[Hitachinaka Seaside Railway Minato Line|Minato Line]], [[:en:Ajigaura Station|Ajigaura Station]] (about 15 minutes on foot) - The terminal station of the Minato Line. Plaque "Sakattsura Isosaki Shrine" written by [[Prince Komatsu Akihito]]]] '''Sakattsura Isosaki Shrine''' (さかつらいそさきじんじゃ) is a [[Shinto shrine]] located in [[Hitachinaka City]], [[Ibaraki Prefecture]]. It is classified as a [[Myōjin Taisha|Myōjin Taisha]] under the [[Engishiki|Engishiki system]]. The former shrine Rank was [[National Middle Shrine|Kokuhei Chūsha]], and it is now a [[Beppyo Shrine]] under the [[Association of Shinto Shrines]]. == Overview == The shrine is situated on a hill facing the [[Pacific Ocean]] in eastern [[Ibaraki Prefecture]]. It is closely related to [[Ōarai Isosaki Shrine]] in [[Ōarai Town]] across the [[Naka River]], and the two shrines form a single faith. == Deities == '''Main deity''' * '''[[Sukunahikona no Mikoto]]''' (少彦名命) *: Known for helping [[Ōkuninushi|Ōnamuchi no Mikoto]] (Ōkuninushi no Mikoto) in creating the land. '''Enshrined deity''' * [[Ōkuninushi|Ōnamuchi no Mikoto]] (大名持命) *: Another name for [[Ōkuninushi no Mikoto]] (大己貴命), the deity of [[Ōarai Isosaki Shrine]], and his divided spirit. He is said to have created the land with the help of Sukunahikona no Mikoto. In the myths found in the [[Kojiki]], [[Nihon Shoki]], and [[Fudoki]], these two deities often appear together in the stories of land creation. Many shrines enshrine this combination of deities. At this shrine, Sukunahikona no Mikoto is also considered [[Ebisu]] of the [[Seven Lucky Gods]], and Ōnamuchi no Mikoto is considered [[Daikokuten]]. == History == === Founding === According to the [[Nihon Montoku Tennō Jitsuroku]], a deity appeared at Ōarai Isosaki in [[Kashima District, Hitachi Province]] in Saikō 3rd year (856). {{quotation| Hitachi Province reports that a new deity has descended at Ōarai Isosaki in Kashima District. Initially, a salt maker saw a shining light in the sea at midnight. The next day, two strange stones appeared on the shore, each about a foot high. The following day, more than twenty small stones appeared around the strange stones, resembling attendants. The stones were vividly colored and shaped like monks, but without ears or eyes. The divine spirit possessed a person and said, "I am Ōnamuchi and Sukunahikona. We finished creating this land and went to the eastern sea, but we have returned to save the people." |Nihon Montoku Tennō Jitsuroku, Saikō 3rd year, December戊戌条}} Thus, Ōkuninushi no Mikoto (Ōnamuchi) was enshrined at Ōarai, and Sukunahikona no Mikoto was enshrined at Sakattsura, marking the founding of the two shrines. The rock formations along the coast near the shrine are tilted about 45 degrees to the south, and the part that tilts to the north is called "Gyaku-retsu" (逆列, Reverse Row), which is said to be the origin of the shrine's name. Later, it came to be known as "Sakattsura" because it enshrined the god of sake (alcohol)[http://www.oyashiro.or.jp/link/0006.html Sakattsura Isosaki Shrine] (Ibaraki Prefecture Shrine Office). === Historical Overview === The [[Engishiki]] lists the shrine as "Hitachi Province Naka District Sakattsura Isosaki Yakushi Bosatsu Shrine" and classifies it as a Myōjin Taisha. The shrine fell into decline during the [[Middle Ages]] and lost its buildings. In the [[Early Modern Period]], the second lord of the [[Mito Domain]], [[Tokugawa Mitsukuni]], initiated the rebuilding of the shrine, and the third lord, [[Tokugawa Tsunaeda]], relocated and restored it to its current location. The old site is said to be near the first torii. In 1885 (Meiji 18), the shrine was Ranked as a [[National Middle Shrine|Kokuhei Chūsha]] under the [[Modern Shrine Rank System]]. It is now officially named "Sakattsura Isosaki Shrine." === Shrine Rankings === * [[Ten'an]] 1st year (857), August 7 - Received official shrine status (Nihon Montoku Tennō Jitsuroku) * Ten'an 1st year (857), October 15 - Granted the title "Yakushi Bosatsu Myōjin" (Nihon Montoku Tennō Jitsuroku) == Grounds == The carving of a squirrel and grapes on the front of the haiden is said to be the work of [[Hidari Jingorō]]. The guardian dogs (komainu) on either side of the second torii were made by a Showa period stone mason named Heikichi Iizuka. The path to the shrine is lined with camellia, tabunoki, and sudajii trees, forming a broadleaf forest that is designated a Natural Monument by Ibaraki Prefecture. The original shrine site is believed to be near the first torii, around the ruins of Hikantei. Designated in 2005. == location Information == '''location''' * [[Ibaraki Prefecture]], [[Hitachinaka City]], Isosaki Town 4607-2 '''Transportation Access''' * Nearest station: [[Hitachinaka Seaside Railway]], [[Hitachinaka Seaside Railway Minato Line|Minato Line]], [[:en:Ajigaura Station|Ajigaura Station]] (about 15 minutes on foot) - The terminal station of the Minato Line. '''Nearby''' * Ruins of Hikantei - Ruins of a pavilion built by the Mito Domain. Designated a Historic Site by Hitachinaka City. * Kanto Place - A scenic spot selected by the lords of the Mito Domain. Designated a Scenic Spot by Hitachinaka City. * Kawagozuka Kofun - Designated a Historic Site by Hitachinaka City. * Hiraiso Cretaceous Layer - Nearby coast. Designated a Natural Monument by Ibaraki Prefecture. == References == {{reflist}} == Related Books == * Anzu Moto, Umeda Yoshihiko, editors and supervisors, "Shinto Dictionary", [[Shinto Shinpōsha]], Plaque "Sakattsura Isosaki Shrine" written by [[Prince Komatsu Akihito]]]] '''Sakattsura Isosaki Shrine''' (さかつらいそさきじんじゃ) is a [[Shinto shrine]] located in [[Hitachinaka City]], [[Ibaraki Prefecture]]. It is classified as a [[Myōjin Taisha|Myōjin Taisha]] under the [[Engishiki|Engishiki system]]. The former shrine Rank was [[National Middle Shrine|Kokuhei Chūsha]], and it is now a [[Beppyo Shrine]] under the [[Association of Shinto Shrines]]. == Overview == The shrine is situated on a hill facing the [[Pacific Ocean]] in eastern [[Ibaraki Prefecture]]. It is closely related to [[Ōarai Isosaki Shrine]] in [[Ōarai Town]] across the [[Naka River]], and the two shrines form a single faith. == Deities == '''Main deity''' * '''[[Sukunahikona no Mikoto]]''' (少彦名命) *: Known for helping [[Ōkuninushi|Ōnamuchi no Mikoto]] (Ōkuninushi no Mikoto) in creating the land. '''Enshrined deity''' * [[Ōkuninushi|Ōnamuchi no Mikoto]] (大名持命) *: Another name for [[Ōkuninushi no Mikoto]] (大己貴命), the deity of [[Ōarai Isosaki Shrine]], and his divided spirit. He is said to have created the land with the help of Sukunahikona no Mikoto. In the myths found in the [[Kojiki]], [[Nihon Shoki]], and [[Fudoki]], these two deities often appear together in the stories of land creation. Many shrines enshrine this combination of deities. At this shrine, Sukunahikona no Mikoto is also considered [[Ebisu]] of the [[Seven Lucky Gods]], and Ōnamuchi no Mikoto is considered [[Daikokuten]]. == History == === Founding === According to the [[Nihon Montoku Tennō Jitsuroku]], a deity appeared at Ōarai Isosaki in [[Kashima District, Hitachi Province]] in Saikō 3rd year (856). {{quotation| Hitachi Province reports that a new deity has descended at Ōarai Isosaki in Kashima District. Initially, a salt maker saw a shining light in the sea at midnight. The next day, two strange stones appeared on the shore, each about a foot high. The following day, more than twenty small stones appeared around the strange stones, resembling attendants. The stones were vividly colored and shaped like monks, but without ears or eyes. The divine spirit possessed a person and said, "I am Ōnamuchi and Sukunahikona. We finished creating this land and went to the eastern sea, but we have returned to save the people." |Nihon Montoku Tennō Jitsuroku, Saikō 3rd year, December戊戌条}} Thus, Ōkuninushi no Mikoto (Ōnamuchi) was enshrined at Ōarai, and Sukunahikona no Mikoto was enshrined at Sakattsura, marking the founding of the two shrines. The rock formations along the coast near the shrine are tilted about 45 degrees to the south, and the part that tilts to the north is called "Gyaku-retsu" (逆列, Reverse Row), which is said to be the origin of the shrine's name. Later, it came to be known as "Sakattsura" because it enshrined the god of sake (alcohol)[http://www.oyashiro.or.jp/link/0006.html Sakattsura Isosaki Shrine] (Ibaraki Prefecture Shrine Office). === Historical Overview === The [[Engishiki]] lists the shrine as "Hitachi Province Naka District Sakattsura Isosaki Yakushi Bosatsu Shrine" and classifies it as a Myōjin Taisha. The shrine fell into decline during the [[Middle Ages]] and lost its buildings. In the [[Early Modern Period]], the second lord of the [[Mito Domain]], [[Tokugawa Mitsukuni]], initiated the rebuilding of the shrine, and the third lord, [[Tokugawa Tsunaeda]], relocated and restored it to its current location. The old site is said to be near the first torii. In 1885 (Meiji 18), the shrine was Ranked as a [[National Middle Shrine|Kokuhei Chūsha]] under the [[Modern Shrine Rank System]]. It is now officially named "Sakattsura Isosaki Shrine." === Shrine Rankings === * [[Ten'an]] 1st year (857), August 7 - Received official shrine status (Nihon Montoku Tennō Jitsuroku) * Ten'an 1st year (857), October 15 - Granted the title "Yakushi Bosatsu Myōjin" (Nihon Montoku Tennō Jitsuroku) == Grounds == The carving of a squirrel and grapes on the front of the haiden is said to be the work of [[Hidari Jingorō]]. The guardian dogs (komainu) on either side of the second torii were made by a Showa period stone mason named Heikichi Iizuka. The path to the shrine is lined with camellia, tabunoki, and sudajii trees, forming a broadleaf forest that is designated a Natural Monument by Ibaraki Prefecture. The original shrine site is believed to be near the first torii, around the ruins of Hikantei. At this shrine, Sukunahikona no Mikoto is also considered [[Ebisu]] of the [[Seven Lucky Gods]], and Ōnamuchi no Mikoto is considered [[Daikokuten]]. == History == === Founding === According to the [[Nihon Montoku Tennō Jitsuroku]], a deity appeared at Ōarai Isosaki in [[Kashima District, Hitachi Province]] in Saikō 3rd year (856). {{quotation| Hitachi Province reports that a new deity has descended at Ōarai Isosaki in Kashima District. Initially, a salt maker saw a shining light in the sea at midnight. The next day, two strange stones appeared on the shore, each about a foot high. The following day, more than twenty small stones appeared around the strange stones, resembling attendants. The stones were vividly colored and shaped like monks, but without ears or eyes. The divine spirit possessed a person and said, "I am Ōnamuchi and Sukunahikona. We finished creating this land and went to the eastern sea, but we have returned to save the people." |Nihon Montoku Tennō Jitsuroku, Saikō 3rd year, December戊戌条}} Thus, Ōkuninushi no Mikoto (Ōnamuchi) was enshrined at Ōarai, and Sukunahikona no Mikoto was enshrined at Sakattsura, marking the founding of the two shrines. The rock formations along the coast near the shrine are tilted about 45 degrees to the south, and the part that tilts to the north is called "Gyaku-retsu" (逆列, Reverse Row), which is said to be the origin of the shrine's name. Later, it came to be known as "Sakattsura" because it enshrined the god of sake (alcohol)[http://www.oyashiro.or.jp/link/0006.html Sakattsura Isosaki Shrine] (Ibaraki Prefecture Shrine Office). === Historical Overview === The [[Engishiki]] lists the shrine as "Hitachi Province Naka District Sakattsura Isosaki Yakushi Bosatsu Shrine" and classifies it as a Myōjin Taisha. The shrine fell into decline during the [[Middle Ages]] and lost its buildings. In the [[Early Modern Period]], the second lord of the [[Mito Domain]], [[Tokugawa Mitsukuni]], initiated the rebuilding of the shrine, and the third lord, [[Tokugawa Tsunaeda]], relocated and restored it to its current location. The old site is said to be near the first torii. In 1885 (Meiji 18), the shrine was Ranked as a [[National Middle Shrine|Kokuhei Chūsha]] under the [[Modern Shrine Rank System]]. It is now officially named "Sakattsura Isosaki Shrine." === Shrine Rankings === * [[Ten'an]] 1st year (857), August 7 - Received official shrine status (Nihon Montoku Tennō Jitsuroku) * Ten'an 1st year (857), October 15 - Granted the title "Yakushi Bosatsu Myōjin" (Nihon Montoku Tennō Jitsuroku) == Grounds == The carving of a squirrel and grapes on the front of the haiden is said to be the work of [[Hidari Jingorō]]. The guardian dogs (komainu) on either side of the second torii were made by a Showa period stone mason named Heikichi Iizuka. The path to the shrine is lined with camellia, tabunoki, and sudajii trees, forming a broadleaf forest that is designated a Natural Monument by Ibaraki Prefecture. Plaque "Sakattsura Isosaki Shrine" written by [[Prince Komatsu Akihito]]]] '''Sakattsura Isosaki Shrine''' (さかつらいそさきじんじゃ) is a [[Shinto shrine]] located in [[Hitachinaka City]], [[Ibaraki Prefecture]]. It is classified as a [[Myōjin Taisha|Myōjin Taisha]] under the [[Engishiki|Engishiki system]]. The former shrine Rank was [[National Middle Shrine|Kokuhei Chūsha]], and it is now a [[Beppyo Shrine]] under the [[Association of Shinto Shrines]]. == Overview == The shrine is situated on a hill facing the [[Pacific Ocean]] in eastern [[Ibaraki Prefecture]]. It is closely related to [[Ōarai Isosaki Shrine]] in [[Ōarai Town]] across the [[Naka River]], and the two shrines form a single faith. == Deities == '''Main deity''' * '''[[Sukunahikona no Mikoto]]''' (少彦名命) *: Known for helping [[Ōkuninushi|Ōnamuchi no Mikoto]] (Ōkuninushi no Mikoto) in creating the land. '''Enshrined deity''' * [[Ōkuninushi|Ōnamuchi no Mikoto]] (大名持命) *: Another name for [[Ōkuninushi no Mikoto]] (大己貴命), the deity of [[Ōarai Isosaki Shrine]], and his divided spirit. He is said to have created the land with the help of Sukunahikona no Mikoto. In the myths found in the [[Kojiki]], [[Nihon Shoki]], and [[Fudoki]], these two deities often appear together in the stories of land creation. Many shrines enshrine this combination of deities. At this shrine, Sukunahikona no Mikoto is also considered [[Ebisu]] of the [[Seven Lucky Gods]], and Ōnamuchi no Mikoto is considered [[Daikokuten]]. == History == === Founding === According to the [[Nihon Montoku Tennō Jitsuroku]], a deity appeared at Ōarai Isosaki in [[Kashima District, Hitachi Province]] in Saikō 3rd year (856). {{quotation| Hitachi Province reports that a new deity has descended at Ōarai Isosaki in Kashima District. Initially, a salt maker saw a shining light in the sea at midnight. The next day, two strange stones appeared on the shore, each about a foot high. The following day, more than twenty small stones appeared around the strange stones, resembling attendants. The stones were vividly colored and shaped like monks, but without ears or eyes. The divine spirit possessed a person and said, "I am Ōnamuchi and Sukunahikona. We finished creating this land and went to the eastern sea, but we have returned to save the people." |Nihon Montoku Tennō Jitsuroku, Saikō 3rd year, December戊戌条}} Thus, Ōkuninushi no Mikoto (Ōnamuchi) was enshrined at Ōarai, and Sukunahikona no Mikoto was enshrined at Sakattsura, marking the founding of the two shrines. The rock formations along the coast near the shrine are tilted about 45 degrees to the south, and the part that tilts to the north is called "Gyaku-retsu" (逆列, Reverse Row), which is said to be the origin of the shrine's name. Later, it came to be known as "Sakattsura" because it enshrined the god of sake (alcohol)[http://www.oyashiro.or.jp/link/0006.html Sakattsura Isosaki Shrine] (Ibaraki Prefecture Shrine Office). === Historical Overview === The [[Engishiki]] lists the shrine as "Hitachi Province Naka District Sakattsura Isosaki Yakushi Bosatsu Shrine" and classifies it as a Myōjin Taisha. The shrine fell into decline during the [[Middle Ages]] and lost its buildings. In the [[Early Modern Period]], the second lord of the [[Mito Domain]], [[Tokugawa Mitsukuni]], initiated the rebuilding of the shrine, and the third lord, [[Tokugawa Tsunaeda]], relocated and restored it to its current location. The old site is said to be near the first torii. In 1885 (Meiji 18), the shrine was Ranked as a [[National Middle Shrine|Kokuhei Chūsha]] under the [[Modern Shrine Rank System]]. It is now officially named "Sakattsura Isosaki Shrine." === Shrine Rankings === * [[Ten'an]] 1st year (857), August 7 - Received official shrine status (Nihon Montoku Tennō Jitsuroku) * Ten'an 1st year (857), October 15 - Granted the title "Yakushi Bosatsu Myōjin" (Nihon Montoku Tennō Jitsuroku) == Grounds == The carving of a squirrel and grapes on the front of the haiden is said to be the work of [[Hidari Jingorō]]. The guardian dogs (komainu) on either side of the second torii were made by a Showa period stone mason named Heikichi Iizuka. The path to the shrine is lined with camellia, tabunoki, and sudajii trees, forming a broadleaf forest that is designated a Natural Monument by Ibaraki Prefecture. The original shrine site is believed to be near the first torii, around the ruins of Hikantei. Designated in 2005. == location Information == '''location''' * [[Ibaraki Prefecture]], [[Hitachinaka City]], Isosaki Town 4607-2 '''Transportation Access''' * Nearest station: [[Hitachinaka Seaside Railway]], [[Hitachinaka Seaside Railway Minato Line|Minato Line]], [[:en:Ajigaura Station|Ajigaura Station]] (about 15 minutes on foot) - The terminal station of the Minato Line. '''Nearby''' * Ruins of Hikantei - Ruins of a pavilion built by the Mito Domain. Plaque "Sakattsura Isosaki Shrine" written by [[Prince Komatsu Akihito]]]] '''Sakattsura Isosaki Shrine''' (さかつらいそさきじんじゃ) is a [[Shinto shrine]] located in [[Hitachinaka City]], [[Ibaraki Prefecture]]. It is classified as a [[Myōjin Taisha|Myōjin Taisha]] under the [[Engishiki|Engishiki system]]. The former shrine Rank was [[National Middle Shrine|Kokuhei Chūsha]], and it is now a [[Beppyo Shrine]] under the [[Association of Shinto Shrines]]. == Overview == The shrine is situated on a hill facing the [[Pacific Ocean]] in eastern [[Ibaraki Prefecture]]. It is closely related to [[Ōarai Isosaki Shrine]] in [[Ōarai Town]] across the [[Naka River]], and the two shrines form a single faith. == Deities == '''Main deity''' * '''[[Sukunahikona no Mikoto]]''' (少彦名命) *: Known for helping [[Ōkuninushi|Ōnamuchi no Mikoto]] (Ōkuninushi no Mikoto) in creating the land. '''Enshrined deity''' * [[Ōkuninushi|Ōnamuchi no Mikoto]] (大名持命) *: Another name for [[Ōkuninushi no Mikoto]] (大己貴命), the deity of [[Ōarai Isosaki Shrine]], and his divided spirit. He is said to have created the land with the help of Sukunahikona no Mikoto. In the myths found in the [[Kojiki]], [[Nihon Shoki]], and [[Fudoki]], these two deities often appear together in the stories of land creation. Many shrines enshrine this combination of deities. At this shrine, Sukunahikona no Mikoto is also considered [[Ebisu]] of the [[Seven Lucky Gods]], and Ōnamuchi no Mikoto is considered [[Daikokuten]]. == History == === Founding === According to the [[Nihon Montoku Tennō Jitsuroku]], a deity appeared at Ōarai Isosaki in [[Kashima District, Hitachi Province]] in Saikō 3rd year (856). {{quotation| Hitachi Province reports that a new deity has descended at Ōarai Isosaki in Kashima District. Initially, a salt maker saw a shining light in the sea at midnight. The next day, two strange stones appeared on the shore, each about a foot high. The following day, more than twenty small stones appeared around the strange stones, resembling attendants. The stones were vividly colored and shaped like monks, but without ears or eyes. The divine spirit possessed a person and said, "I am Ōnamuchi and Sukunahikona. We finished creating this land and went to the eastern sea, but we have returned to save the people." |Nihon Montoku Tennō Jitsuroku, Saikō 3rd year, December戊戌条}} Thus, Ōkuninushi no Mikoto (Ōnamuchi) was enshrined at Ōarai, and Sukunahikona no Mikoto was enshrined at Sakattsura, marking the founding of the two shrines. The rock formations along the coast near the shrine are tilted about 45 degrees to the south, and the part that tilts to the north is called "Gyaku-retsu" (逆列, Reverse Row), which is said to be the origin of the shrine's name. Later, it came to be known as "Sakattsura" because it enshrined the god of sake (alcohol)[http://www.oyashiro.or.jp/link/0006.html Sakattsura Isosaki Shrine] (Ibaraki Prefecture Shrine Office). === Historical Overview === The [[Engishiki]] lists the shrine as "Hitachi Province Naka District Sakattsura Isosaki Yakushi Bosatsu Shrine" and classifies it as a Myōjin Taisha. The shrine fell into decline during the [[Middle Ages]] and lost its buildings. In the [[Early Modern Period]], the second lord of the [[Mito Domain]], [[Tokugawa Mitsukuni]], initiated the rebuilding of the shrine, and the third lord, [[Tokugawa Tsunaeda]], relocated and restored it to its current location. The old site is said to be near the first torii. In 1885 (Meiji 18), the shrine was Ranked as a [[National Middle Shrine|Kokuhei Chūsha]] under the [[Modern Shrine Rank System]]. It is now officially named "Sakattsura Isosaki Shrine." === Shrine Rankings === * [[Ten'an]] 1st year (857), August 7 - Received official shrine status (Nihon Montoku Tennō Jitsuroku) * Ten'an 1st year (857), October 15 - Granted the title "Yakushi Bosatsu Myōjin" (Nihon Montoku Tennō Jitsuroku) == Grounds == The carving of a squirrel and grapes on the front of the haiden is said to be the work of [[Hidari Jingorō]]. The guardian dogs (komainu) on either side of the second torii were made by a Showa period stone mason named Heikichi Iizuka. The path to the shrine is lined with camellia, tabunoki, and sudajii trees, forming a broadleaf forest that is designated a Natural Monument by Ibaraki Prefecture. The original shrine site is believed to be near the first torii, around the ruins of Hikantei. Plaque "Sakattsura Isosaki Shrine" written by [[Prince Komatsu Akihito]]]] '''Sakattsura Isosaki Shrine''' (さかつらいそさきじんじゃ) is a [[Shinto shrine]] located in [[Hitachinaka City]], [[Ibaraki Prefecture]]. It is classified as a [[Myōjin Taisha|Myōjin Taisha]] under the [[Engishiki|Engishiki system]]. The former shrine Rank was [[National Middle Shrine|Kokuhei Chūsha]], and it is now a [[Beppyo Shrine]] under the [[Association of Shinto Shrines]]. == Overview == The shrine is situated on a hill facing the [[Pacific Ocean]] in eastern [[Ibaraki Prefecture]]. It is closely related to [[Ōarai Isosaki Shrine]] in [[Ōarai Town]] across the [[Naka River]], and the two shrines form a single faith. == Deities == '''Main deity''' * '''[[Sukunahikona no Mikoto]]''' (少彦名命) *: Known for helping [[Ōkuninushi|Ōnamuchi no Mikoto]] (Ōkuninushi no Mikoto) in creating the land. '''Enshrined deity''' * [[Ōkuninushi|Ōnamuchi no Mikoto]] (大名持命) *: Another name for [[Ōkuninushi no Mikoto]] (大己貴命), the deity of [[Ōarai Isosaki Shrine]], and his divided spirit. He is said to have created the land with the help of Sukunahikona no Mikoto. In the myths found in the [[Kojiki]], [[Nihon Shoki]], and [[Fudoki]], these two deities often appear together in the stories of land creation. Many shrines enshrine this combination of deities. At this shrine, Sukunahikona no Mikoto is also considered [[Ebisu]] of the [[Seven Lucky Gods]], and Ōnamuchi no Mikoto is considered [[Daikokuten]]. == History == === Founding === According to the [[Nihon Montoku Tennō Jitsuroku]], a deity appeared at Ōarai Isosaki in [[Kashima District, Hitachi Province]] in Saikō 3rd year (856). {{quotation| Hitachi Province reports that a new deity has descended at Ōarai Isosaki in Kashima District. Initially, a salt maker saw a shining light in the sea at midnight. The next day, two strange stones appeared on the shore, each about a foot high. The following day, more than twenty small stones appeared around the strange stones, resembling attendants. The stones were vividly colored and shaped like monks, but without ears or eyes. The divine spirit possessed a person and said, "I am Ōnamuchi and Sukunahikona. We finished creating this land and went to the eastern sea, but we have returned to save the people." |Nihon Montoku Tennō Jitsuroku, Saikō 3rd year, December戊戌条}} Thus, Ōkuninushi no Mikoto (Ōnamuchi) was enshrined at Ōarai, and Sukunahikona no Mikoto was enshrined at Sakattsura, marking the founding of the two shrines. The rock formations along the coast near the shrine are tilted about 45 degrees to the south, and the part that tilts to the north is called "Gyaku-retsu" (逆列, Reverse Row), which is said to be the origin of the shrine's name. Later, it came to be known as "Sakattsura" because it enshrined the god of sake (alcohol)[http://www.oyashiro.or.jp/link/0006.html Sakattsura Isosaki Shrine] (Ibaraki Prefecture Shrine Office). === Historical Overview === The [[Engishiki]] lists the shrine as "Hitachi Province Naka District Sakattsura Isosaki Yakushi Bosatsu Shrine" and classifies it as a Myōjin Taisha. The shrine fell into decline during the [[Middle Ages]] and lost its buildings. In the [[Early Modern Period]], the second lord of the [[Mito Domain]], [[Tokugawa Mitsukuni]], initiated the rebuilding of the shrine, and the third lord, [[Tokugawa Tsunaeda]], relocated and restored it to its current location. The old site is said to be near the first torii. In 1885 (Meiji 18), the shrine was Ranked as a [[National Middle Shrine|Kokuhei Chūsha]] under the [[Modern Shrine Rank System]]. It is now officially named "Sakattsura Isosaki Shrine." === Shrine Rankings === * [[Ten'an]] 1st year (857), August 7 - Received official shrine status (Nihon Montoku Tennō Jitsuroku) * Ten'an 1st year (857), October 15 - Granted the title "Yakushi Bosatsu Myōjin" (Nihon Montoku Tennō Jitsuroku) == Grounds == The carving of a squirrel and grapes on the front of the haiden is said to be the work of [[Hidari Jingorō]]. The guardian dogs (komainu) on either side of the second torii were made by a Showa period stone mason named Heikichi Iizuka. The path to the shrine is lined with camellia, tabunoki, and sudajii trees, forming a broadleaf forest that is designated a Natural Monument by Ibaraki Prefecture. The original shrine site is believed to be near the first torii, around the ruins of Hikantei. File:Sakattsura Isosaki Shrine main hall.JPG|main hall File:Sakattsura Isosaki Shrine Worship Hall.JPG|Worship Hall File:Sakattsura Isosaki Shrine Stone where Tokugawa Nariaki sat.JPG|Stone where [[Tokugawa Nariaki]] sat File:Sakattsura Isosaki Shrine Second Torii.JPG|Second Torii File:Sakattsura Isosaki Shrine Approach.JPG|Approach (Prefectural Natural Monument) == Auxiliary Shrines == [[File:Sakattsura Chinjusha (Auxiliary Shrine of Sakattsura Isosaki Shrine).JPG|thumb|200px|Sakattsura Chinjusha]] [[File:Sakattsura Isosaki Shrine Auxiliary Shrines.JPG|thumb|200px|Five Auxiliary Shrines]] * Sakattsura Chinjusha (さかつらちんれいしゃ) ** Enshrined deity: 506 war dead from the [[Russo-Japanese War]] to [[World War II]] *: Located north of the main hall. * Inari Shrine - Enshrined deity: [[Ukanomitama|Ukanomitama no Mikoto]] * Tenmangū - Enshrined deity: [[Sugawara no Michizane]] * Kotohira Shrine - Enshrined deity: [[Ōmononushi|Ōmononushi no Mikoto]] * Fuji Shrine - Enshrined deity: [[Konohanasakuya-hime]], worshipped as a deity of safe childbirth. * Water Shrine - Enshrined deity: [[Mizuhanome|Mizuhanome no Mikoto]] == Cultural Properties == === Ibaraki Prefecture Designated Natural Monument === * Sakattsura Isosaki Shrine Tree Grove - The broadleaf forest of camellia, tabunoki, and sudajii trees along the approach and surrounding the grounds. Designated in 2005. == location Information == '''location''' * [[Ibaraki Prefecture]], [[Hitachinaka City]], Isosaki Town 4607-2 '''Transportation Access''' * Nearest station: [[Hitachinaka Seaside Railway]], [[Hitachinaka Seaside Railway Minato Line|Minato Line]], [[:en:Ajigaura Station|Ajigaura Station]] (about 15 minutes on foot) - The terminal station of the Minato Line. '''Nearby''' * Ruins of Hikantei - Ruins of a pavilion built by the Mito Domain. Designated a Historic Site by Hitachinaka City. * Kanto Place - A scenic spot selected by the lords of the Mito Domain. Designated a Scenic Spot by Hitachinaka City. * Kawagozuka Kofun - Designated a Historic Site by Hitachinaka City. * Hiraiso Cretaceous Layer - Nearby coast. Designated a Natural Monument by Ibaraki Prefecture. == References == {{reflist}} == Related Books == * Anzu Moto, Umeda Yoshihiko, editors and supervisors, "Shinto Dictionary", [[Shinto Shinpōsha]], Plaque "Sakattsura Isosaki Shrine" written by [[Prince Komatsu Akihito]]]] '''Sakattsura Isosaki Shrine''' (さかつらいそさきじんじゃ) is a [[Shinto shrine]] located in [[Hitachinaka City]], [[Ibaraki Prefecture]]. It is classified as a [[Myōjin Taisha|Myōjin Taisha]] under the [[Engishiki|Engishiki system]]. The former shrine Rank was [[National Middle Shrine|Kokuhei Chūsha]], and it is now a [[Beppyo Shrine]] under the [[Association of Shinto Shrines]]. == Overview == The shrine is situated on a hill facing the [[Pacific Ocean]] in eastern [[Ibaraki Prefecture]]. It is closely related to [[Ōarai Isosaki Shrine]] in [[Ōarai Town]] across the [[Naka River]], and the two shrines form a single faith. == Deities == '''Main deity''' * '''[[Sukunahikona no Mikoto]]''' (少彦名命) *: Known for helping [[Ōkuninushi|Ōnamuchi no Mikoto]] (Ōkuninushi no Mikoto) in creating the land. '''Enshrined deity''' * [[Ōkuninushi|Ōnamuchi no Mikoto]] (大名持命) *: Another name for [[Ōkuninushi no Mikoto]] (大己貴命), the deity of [[Ōarai Isosaki Shrine]], and his divided spirit. He is said to have created the land with the help of Sukunahikona no Mikoto. In the myths found in the [[Kojiki]], [[Nihon Shoki]], and [[Fudoki]], these two deities often appear together in the stories of land creation. Many shrines enshrine this combination of deities. At this shrine, Sukunahikona no Mikoto is also considered [[Ebisu]] of the [[Seven Lucky Gods]], and Ōnamuchi no Mikoto is considered [[Daikokuten]]. == History == === Founding === According to the [[Nihon Montoku Tennō Jitsuroku]], a deity appeared at Ōarai Isosaki in [[Kashima District, Hitachi Province]] in Saikō 3rd year (856). {{quotation| Hitachi Province reports that a new deity has descended at Ōarai Isosaki in Kashima District. Initially, a salt maker saw a shining light in the sea at midnight. The next day, two strange stones appeared on the shore, each about a foot high. The following day, more than twenty small stones appeared around the strange stones, resembling attendants. The stones were vividly colored and shaped like monks, but without ears or eyes. The divine spirit possessed a person and said, "I am Ōnamuchi and Sukunahikona. We finished creating this land and went to the eastern sea, but we have returned to save the people." |Nihon Montoku Tennō Jitsuroku, Saikō 3rd year, December戊戌条}} Thus, Ōkuninushi no Mikoto (Ōnamuchi) was enshrined at Ōarai, and Sukunahikona no Mikoto was enshrined at Sakattsura, marking the founding of the two shrines. The rock formations along the coast near the shrine are tilted about 45 degrees to the south, and the part that tilts to the north is called "Gyaku-retsu" (逆列, Reverse Row), which is said to be the origin of the shrine's name. Later, it came to be known as "Sakattsura" because it enshrined the god of sake (alcohol)[http://www.oyashiro.or.jp/link/0006.html Sakattsura Isosaki Shrine] (Ibaraki Prefecture Shrine Office). === Historical Overview === The [[Engishiki]] lists the shrine as "Hitachi Province Naka District Sakattsura Isosaki Yakushi Bosatsu Shrine" and classifies it as a Myōjin Taisha. The shrine fell into decline during the [[Middle Ages]] and lost its buildings. In the [[Early Modern Period]], the second lord of the [[Mito Domain]], [[Tokugawa Mitsukuni]], initiated the rebuilding of the shrine, and the third lord, [[Tokugawa Tsunaeda]], relocated and restored it to its current location. The old site is said to be near the first torii. In 1885 (Meiji 18), the shrine was Ranked as a [[National Middle Shrine|Kokuhei Chūsha]] under the [[Modern Shrine Rank System]]. It is now officially named "Sakattsura Isosaki Shrine." === Shrine Rankings === * [[Ten'an]] 1st year (857), August 7 - Received official shrine status (Nihon Montoku Tennō Jitsuroku) * Ten'an 1st year (857), October 15 - Granted the title "Yakushi Bosatsu Myōjin" (Nihon Montoku Tennō Jitsuroku) == Grounds == The carving of a squirrel and grapes on the front of the haiden is said to be the work of [[Hidari Jingorō]]. The guardian dogs (komainu) on either side of the second torii were made by a Showa period stone mason named Heikichi Iizuka. The path to the shrine is lined with camellia, tabunoki, and sudajii trees, forming a broadleaf forest that is designated a Natural Monument by Ibaraki Prefecture. The original shrine site is believed to be near the first torii, around the ruins of Hikantei. Plaque "Sakattsura Isosaki Shrine" written by [[Prince Komatsu Akihito]]]] '''Sakattsura Isosaki Shrine''' (さかつらいそさきじんじゃ) is a [[Shinto shrine]] located in [[Hitachinaka City]], [[Ibaraki Prefecture]]. It is classified as a [[Myōjin Taisha|Myōjin Taisha]] under the [[Engishiki|Engishiki system]]. The former shrine Rank was [[National Middle Shrine|Kokuhei Chūsha]], and it is now a [[Beppyo Shrine]] under the [[Association of Shinto Shrines]]. == Overview == The shrine is situated on a hill facing the [[Pacific Ocean]] in eastern [[Ibaraki Prefecture]]. It is closely related to [[Ōarai Isosaki Shrine]] in [[Ōarai Town]] across the [[Naka River]], and the two shrines form a single faith. == Deities == '''Main deity''' * '''[[Sukunahikona no Mikoto]]''' (少彦名命) *: Known for helping [[Ōkuninushi|Ōnamuchi no Mikoto]] (Ōkuninushi no Mikoto) in creating the land. '''Enshrined deity''' * [[Ōkuninushi|Ōnamuchi no Mikoto]] (大名持命) *: Another name for [[Ōkuninushi no Mikoto]] (大己貴命), the deity of [[Ōarai Isosaki Shrine]], and his divided spirit. He is said to have created the land with the help of Sukunahikona no Mikoto. In the myths found in the [[Kojiki]], [[Nihon Shoki]], and [[Fudoki]], these two deities often appear together in the stories of land creation. Many shrines enshrine this combination of deities. At this shrine, Sukunahikona no Mikoto is also considered [[Ebisu]] of the [[Seven Lucky Gods]], and Ōnamuchi no Mikoto is considered [[Daikokuten]]. == History == === Founding === According to the [[Nihon Montoku Tennō Jitsuroku]], a deity appeared at Ōarai Isosaki in [[Kashima District, Hitachi Province]] in Saikō 3rd year (856). {{quotation| Hitachi Province reports that a new deity has descended at Ōarai Isosaki in Kashima District. Initially, a salt maker saw a shining light in the sea at midnight. The next day, two strange stones appeared on the shore, each about a foot high. The following day, more than twenty small stones appeared around the strange stones, resembling attendants. The stones were vividly colored and shaped like monks, but without ears or eyes. The divine spirit possessed a person and said, "I am Ōnamuchi and Sukunahikona. We finished creating this land and went to the eastern sea, but we have returned to save the people." |Nihon Montoku Tennō Jitsuroku, Saikō 3rd year, December戊戌条}} Thus, Ōkuninushi no Mikoto (Ōnamuchi) was enshrined at Ōarai, and Sukunahikona no Mikoto was enshrined at Sakattsura, marking the founding of the two shrines. The rock formations along the coast near the shrine are tilted about 45 degrees to the south, and the part that tilts to the north is called "Gyaku-retsu" (逆列, Reverse Row), which is said to be the origin of the shrine's name. Later, it came to be known as "Sakattsura" because it enshrined the god of sake (alcohol)[http://www.oyashiro.or.jp/link/0006.html Sakattsura Isosaki Shrine] (Ibaraki Prefecture Shrine Office). === Historical Overview === The [[Engishiki]] lists the shrine as "Hitachi Province Naka District Sakattsura Isosaki Yakushi Bosatsu Shrine" and classifies it as a Myōjin Taisha. The shrine fell into decline during the [[Middle Ages]] and lost its buildings. In the [[Early Modern Period]], the second lord of the [[Mito Domain]], [[Tokugawa Mitsukuni]], initiated the rebuilding of the shrine, and the third lord, [[Tokugawa Tsunaeda]], relocated and restored it to its current location. The old site is said to be near the first torii. In 1885 (Meiji 18), the shrine was Ranked as a [[National Middle Shrine|Kokuhei Chūsha]] under the [[Modern Shrine Rank System]]. It is now officially named "Sakattsura Isosaki Shrine." === Shrine Rankings === * [[Ten'an]] 1st year (857), August 7 - Received official shrine status (Nihon Montoku Tennō Jitsuroku) * Ten'an 1st year (857), October 15 - Granted the title "Yakushi Bosatsu Myōjin" (Nihon Montoku Tennō Jitsuroku) == Grounds == The carving of a squirrel and grapes on the front of the haiden is said to be the work of [[Hidari Jingorō]]. The guardian dogs (komainu) on either side of the second torii were made by a Showa period stone mason named Heikichi Iizuka. The path to the shrine is lined with camellia, tabunoki, and sudajii trees, forming a broadleaf forest that is designated a Natural Monument by Ibaraki Prefecture. The original shrine site is believed to be near the first torii, around the ruins of Hikantei. It is closely related to [[Ōarai Isosaki Shrine]] in [[Ōarai Town]] across the [[Naka River]], and the two shrines form a single faith. == Deities == '''Main deity''' * '''[[Sukunahikona no Mikoto]]''' (少彦名命) *: Known for helping [[Ōkuninushi|Ōnamuchi no Mikoto]] (Ōkuninushi no Mikoto) in creating the land. '''Enshrined deity''' * [[Ōkuninushi|Ōnamuchi no Mikoto]] (大名持命) *: Another name for [[Ōkuninushi no Mikoto]] (大己貴命), the deity of [[Ōarai Isosaki Shrine]], and his divided spirit. He is said to have created the land with the help of Sukunahikona no Mikoto. In the myths found in the [[Kojiki]], [[Nihon Shoki]], and [[Fudoki]], these two deities often appear together in the stories of land creation. Many shrines enshrine this combination of deities. At this shrine, Sukunahikona no Mikoto is also considered [[Ebisu]] of the [[Seven Lucky Gods]], and Ōnamuchi no Mikoto is considered [[Daikokuten]]. == History == === Founding === According to the [[Nihon Montoku Tennō Jitsuroku]], a deity appeared at Ōarai Isosaki in [[Kashima District, Hitachi Province]] in Saikō 3rd year (856). {{quotation| Hitachi Province reports that a new deity has descended at Ōarai Isosaki in Kashima District. Initially, a salt maker saw a shining light in the sea at midnight. The next day, two strange stones appeared on the shore, each about a foot high. The following day, more than twenty small stones appeared around the strange stones, resembling attendants. The stones were vividly colored and shaped like monks, but without ears or eyes. The divine spirit possessed a person and said, "I am Ōnamuchi and Sukunahikona. We finished creating this land and went to the eastern sea, but we have returned to save the people." |Nihon Montoku Tennō Jitsuroku, Saikō 3rd year, December戊戌条}} Thus, Ōkuninushi no Mikoto (Ōnamuchi) was enshrined at Ōarai, and Sukunahikona no Mikoto was enshrined at Sakattsura, marking the founding of the two shrines. The rock formations along the coast near the shrine are tilted about 45 degrees to the south, and the part that tilts to the north is called "Gyaku-retsu" (逆列, Reverse Row), which is said to be the origin of the shrine's name. Later, it came to be known as "Sakattsura" because it enshrined the god of sake (alcohol)[http://www.oyashiro.or.jp/link/0006.html Sakattsura Isosaki Shrine] (Ibaraki Prefecture Shrine Office). === Historical Overview === The [[Engishiki]] lists the shrine as "Hitachi Province Naka District Sakattsura Isosaki Yakushi Bosatsu Shrine" and classifies it as a Myōjin Taisha. The shrine fell into decline during the [[Middle Ages]] and lost its buildings. In the [[Early Modern Period]], the second lord of the [[Mito Domain]], [[Tokugawa Mitsukuni]], initiated the rebuilding of the shrine, and the third lord, [[Tokugawa Tsunaeda]], relocated and restored it to its current location. The old site is said to be near the first torii. In 1885 (Meiji 18), the shrine was Ranked as a [[National Middle Shrine|Kokuhei Chūsha]] under the [[Modern Shrine Rank System]]. It is now officially named "Sakattsura Isosaki Shrine." === Shrine Rankings === * [[Ten'an]] 1st year (857), August 7 - Received official shrine status (Nihon Montoku Tennō Jitsuroku) * Ten'an 1st year (857), October 15 - Granted the title "Yakushi Bosatsu Myōjin" (Nihon Montoku Tennō Jitsuroku) == Grounds == The carving of a squirrel and grapes on the front of the haiden is said to be the work of [[Hidari Jingorō]]. The guardian dogs (komainu) on either side of the second torii were made by a Showa period stone mason named Heikichi Iizuka. The path to the shrine is lined with camellia, tabunoki, and sudajii trees, forming a broadleaf forest that is designated a Natural Monument by Ibaraki Prefecture. The original shrine site is believed to be near the first torii, around the ruins of Hikantei. Plaque "Sakattsura Isosaki Shrine" written by [[Prince Komatsu Akihito]]]] '''Sakattsura Isosaki Shrine''' (さかつらいそさきじんじゃ) is a [[Shinto shrine]] located in [[Hitachinaka City]], [[Ibaraki Prefecture]]. It is classified as a [[Myōjin Taisha|Myōjin Taisha]] under the [[Engishiki|Engishiki system]]. The former shrine Rank was [[National Middle Shrine|Kokuhei Chūsha]], and it is now a [[Beppyo Shrine]] under the [[Association of Shinto Shrines]]. == Overview == The shrine is situated on a hill facing the [[Pacific Ocean]] in eastern [[Ibaraki Prefecture]]. It is closely related to [[Ōarai Isosaki Shrine]] in [[Ōarai Town]] across the [[Naka River]], and the two shrines form a single faith. == Deities == '''Main deity''' * '''[[Sukunahikona no Mikoto]]''' (少彦名命) *: Known for helping [[Ōkuninushi|Ōnamuchi no Mikoto]] (Ōkuninushi no Mikoto) in creating the land. '''Enshrined deity''' * [[Ōkuninushi|Ōnamuchi no Mikoto]] (大名持命) *: Another name for [[Ōkuninushi no Mikoto]] (大己貴命), the deity of [[Ōarai Isosaki Shrine]], and his divided spirit. He is said to have created the land with the help of Sukunahikona no Mikoto. In the myths found in the [[Kojiki]], [[Nihon Shoki]], and [[Fudoki]], these two deities often appear together in the stories of land creation. Many shrines enshrine this combination of deities. At this shrine, Sukunahikona no Mikoto is also considered [[Ebisu]] of the [[Seven Lucky Gods]], and Ōnamuchi no Mikoto is considered [[Daikokuten]]. == History == === Founding === According to the [[Nihon Montoku Tennō Jitsuroku]], a deity appeared at Ōarai Isosaki in [[Kashima District, Hitachi Province]] in Saikō 3rd year (856). {{quotation| Hitachi Province reports that a new deity has descended at Ōarai Isosaki in Kashima District. Initially, a salt maker saw a shining light in the sea at midnight. The next day, two strange stones appeared on the shore, each about a foot high. The following day, more than twenty small stones appeared around the strange stones, resembling attendants. The stones were vividly colored and shaped like monks, but without ears or eyes. The divine spirit possessed a person and said, "I am Ōnamuchi and Sukunahikona. We finished creating this land and went to the eastern sea, but we have returned to save the people." |Nihon Montoku Tennō Jitsuroku, Saikō 3rd year, December戊戌条}} Thus, Ōkuninushi no Mikoto (Ōnamuchi) was enshrined at Ōarai, and Sukunahikona no Mikoto was enshrined at Sakattsura, marking the founding of the two shrines. The rock formations along the coast near the shrine are tilted about 45 degrees to the south, and the part that tilts to the north is called "Gyaku-retsu" (逆列, Reverse Row), which is said to be the origin of the shrine's name. Later, it came to be known as "Sakattsura" because it enshrined the god of sake (alcohol)[http://www.oyashiro.or.jp/link/0006.html Sakattsura Isosaki Shrine] (Ibaraki Prefecture Shrine Office). === Historical Overview === The [[Engishiki]] lists the shrine as "Hitachi Province Naka District Sakattsura Isosaki Yakushi Bosatsu Shrine" and classifies it as a Myōjin Taisha. The shrine fell into decline during the [[Middle Ages]] and lost its buildings. In the [[Early Modern Period]], the second lord of the [[Mito Domain]], [[Tokugawa Mitsukuni]], initiated the rebuilding of the shrine, and the third lord, [[Tokugawa Tsunaeda]], relocated and restored it to its current location. The old site is said to be near the first torii. In 1885 (Meiji 18), the shrine was Ranked as a [[National Middle Shrine|Kokuhei Chūsha]] under the [[Modern Shrine Rank System]]. It is now officially named "Sakattsura Isosaki Shrine." === Shrine Rankings === * [[Ten'an]] 1st year (857), August 7 - Received official shrine status (Nihon Montoku Tennō Jitsuroku) * Ten'an 1st year (857), October 15 - Granted the title "Yakushi Bosatsu Myōjin" (Nihon Montoku Tennō Jitsuroku) == Grounds == The carving of a squirrel and grapes on the front of the haiden is said to be the work of [[Hidari Jingorō]]. The guardian dogs (komainu) on either side of the second torii were made by a Showa period stone mason named Heikichi Iizuka. The path to the shrine is lined with camellia, tabunoki, and sudajii trees, forming a broadleaf forest that is designated a Natural Monument by Ibaraki Prefecture. The original shrine site is believed to be near the first torii, around the ruins of Hikantei. Plaque "Sakattsura Isosaki Shrine" written by [[Prince Komatsu Akihito]]]] '''Sakattsura Isosaki Shrine''' (さかつらいそさきじんじゃ) is a [[Shinto shrine]] located in [[Hitachinaka City]], [[Ibaraki Prefecture]]. It is classified as a [[Myōjin Taisha|Myōjin Taisha]] under the [[Engishiki|Engishiki system]]. The former shrine Rank was [[National Middle Shrine|Kokuhei Chūsha]], and it is now a [[Beppyo Shrine]] under the [[Association of Shinto Shrines]]. == Overview == The shrine is situated on a hill facing the [[Pacific Ocean]] in eastern [[Ibaraki Prefecture]]. It is closely related to [[Ōarai Isosaki Shrine]] in [[Ōarai Town]] across the [[Naka River]], and the two shrines form a single faith. == Deities == '''Main deity''' * '''[[Sukunahikona no Mikoto]]''' (少彦名命) *: Known for helping [[Ōkuninushi|Ōnamuchi no Mikoto]] (Ōkuninushi no Mikoto) in creating the land. '''Enshrined deity''' * [[Ōkuninushi|Ōnamuchi no Mikoto]] (大名持命) *: Another name for [[Ōkuninushi no Mikoto]] (大己貴命), the deity of [[Ōarai Isosaki Shrine]], and his divided spirit. He is said to have created the land with the help of Sukunahikona no Mikoto. In the myths found in the [[Kojiki]], [[Nihon Shoki]], and [[Fudoki]], these two deities often appear together in the stories of land creation. Many shrines enshrine this combination of deities. At this shrine, Sukunahikona no Mikoto is also considered [[Ebisu]] of the [[Seven Lucky Gods]], and Ōnamuchi no Mikoto is considered [[Daikokuten]]. == History == === Founding === According to the [[Nihon Montoku Tennō Jitsuroku]], a deity appeared at Ōarai Isosaki in [[Kashima District, Hitachi Province]] in Saikō 3rd year (856). {{quotation| Hitachi Province reports that a new deity has descended at Ōarai Isosaki in Kashima District. Initially, a salt maker saw a shining light in the sea at midnight. The next day, two strange stones appeared on the shore, each about a foot high. The following day, more than twenty small stones appeared around the strange stones, resembling attendants. The stones were vividly colored and shaped like monks, but without ears or eyes. The divine spirit possessed a person and said, "I am Ōnamuchi and Sukunahikona. We finished creating this land and went to the eastern sea, but we have returned to save the people." |Nihon Montoku Tennō Jitsuroku, Saikō 3rd year, December戊戌条}} Thus, Ōkuninushi no Mikoto (Ōnamuchi) was enshrined at Ōarai, and Sukunahikona no Mikoto was enshrined at Sakattsura, marking the founding of the two shrines. The rock formations along the coast near the shrine are tilted about 45 degrees to the south, and the part that tilts to the north is called "Gyaku-retsu" (逆列, Reverse Row), which is said to be the origin of the shrine's name. Later, it came to be known as "Sakattsura" because it enshrined the god of sake (alcohol)[http://www.oyashiro.or.jp/link/0006.html Sakattsura Isosaki Shrine] (Ibaraki Prefecture Shrine Office). === Historical Overview === The [[Engishiki]] lists the shrine as "Hitachi Province Naka District Sakattsura Isosaki Yakushi Bosatsu Shrine" and classifies it as a Myōjin Taisha. The shrine fell into decline during the [[Middle Ages]] and lost its buildings. In the [[Early Modern Period]], the second lord of the [[Mito Domain]], [[Tokugawa Mitsukuni]], initiated the rebuilding of the shrine, and the third lord, [[Tokugawa Tsunaeda]], relocated and restored it to its current location. The old site is said to be near the first torii. In 1885 (Meiji 18), the shrine was Ranked as a [[National Middle Shrine|Kokuhei Chūsha]] under the [[Modern Shrine Rank System]]. It is now officially named "Sakattsura Isosaki Shrine." === Shrine Rankings === * [[Ten'an]] 1st year (857), August 7 - Received official shrine status (Nihon Montoku Tennō Jitsuroku) * Ten'an 1st year (857), October 15 - Granted the title "Yakushi Bosatsu Myōjin" (Nihon Montoku Tennō Jitsuroku) == Grounds == The carving of a squirrel and grapes on the front of the haiden is said to be the work of [[Hidari Jingorō]]. The guardian dogs (komainu) on either side of the second torii were made by a Showa period stone mason named Heikichi Iizuka. The path to the shrine is lined with camellia, tabunoki, and sudajii trees, forming a broadleaf forest that is designated a Natural Monument by Ibaraki Prefecture. The original shrine site is believed to be near the first torii, around the ruins of Hikantei. Plaque "Sakattsura Isosaki Shrine" written by [[Prince Komatsu Akihito]]]] '''Sakattsura Isosaki Shrine''' (さかつらいそさきじんじゃ) is a [[Shinto shrine]] located in [[Hitachinaka City]], [[Ibaraki Prefecture]]. It is classified as a [[Myōjin Taisha|Myōjin Taisha]] under the [[Engishiki|Engishiki system]]. The former shrine Rank was [[National Middle Shrine|Kokuhei Chūsha]], and it is now a [[Beppyo Shrine]] under the [[Association of Shinto Shrines]]. == Overview == The shrine is situated on a hill facing the [[Pacific Ocean]] in eastern [[Ibaraki Prefecture]]. It is closely related to [[Ōarai Isosaki Shrine]] in [[Ōarai Town]] across the [[Naka River]], and the two shrines form a single faith. == Deities == '''Main deity''' * '''[[Sukunahikona no Mikoto]]''' (少彦名命) *: Known for helping [[Ōkuninushi|Ōnamuchi no Mikoto]] (Ōkuninushi no Mikoto) in creating the land. '''Enshrined deity''' * [[Ōkuninushi|Ōnamuchi no Mikoto]] (大名持命) *: Another name for [[Ōkuninushi no Mikoto]] (大己貴命), the deity of [[Ōarai Isosaki Shrine]], and his divided spirit. He is said to have created the land with the help of Sukunahikona no Mikoto. In the myths found in the [[Kojiki]], [[Nihon Shoki]], and [[Fudoki]], these two deities often appear together in the stories of land creation. Many shrines enshrine this combination of deities. At this shrine, Sukunahikona no Mikoto is also considered [[Ebisu]] of the [[Seven Lucky Gods]], and Ōnamuchi no Mikoto is considered [[Daikokuten]]. == History == === Founding === According to the [[Nihon Montoku Tennō Jitsuroku]], a deity appeared at Ōarai Isosaki in [[Kashima District, Hitachi Province]] in Saikō 3rd year (856). {{quotation| Hitachi Province reports that a new deity has descended at Ōarai Isosaki in Kashima District. Initially, a salt maker saw a shining light in the sea at midnight. The next day, two strange stones appeared on the shore, each about a foot high. The following day, more than twenty small stones appeared around the strange stones, resembling attendants. The stones were vividly colored and shaped like monks, but without ears or eyes. The divine spirit possessed a person and said, "I am Ōnamuchi and Sukunahikona. We finished creating this land and went to the eastern sea, but we have returned to save the people." |Nihon Montoku Tennō Jitsuroku, Saikō 3rd year, December戊戌条}} Thus, Ōkuninushi no Mikoto (Ōnamuchi) was enshrined at Ōarai, and Sukunahikona no Mikoto was enshrined at Sakattsura, marking the founding of the two shrines. The rock formations along the coast near the shrine are tilted about 45 degrees to the south, and the part that tilts to the north is called "Gyaku-retsu" (逆列, Reverse Row), which is said to be the origin of the shrine's name. Later, it came to be known as "Sakattsura" because it enshrined the god of sake (alcohol)[http://www.oyashiro.or.jp/link/0006.html Sakattsura Isosaki Shrine] (Ibaraki Prefecture Shrine Office). === Historical Overview === The [[Engishiki]] lists the shrine as "Hitachi Province Naka District Sakattsura Isosaki Yakushi Bosatsu Shrine" and classifies it as a Myōjin Taisha. The shrine fell into decline during the [[Middle Ages]] and lost its buildings. In the [[Early Modern Period]], the second lord of the [[Mito Domain]], [[Tokugawa Mitsukuni]], initiated the rebuilding of the shrine, and the third lord, [[Tokugawa Tsunaeda]], relocated and restored it to its current location. The old site is said to be near the first torii. In 1885 (Meiji 18), the shrine was Ranked as a [[National Middle Shrine|Kokuhei Chūsha]] under the [[Modern Shrine Rank System]]. It is now officially named "Sakattsura Isosaki Shrine." === Shrine Rankings === * [[Ten'an]] 1st year (857), August 7 - Received official shrine status (Nihon Montoku Tennō Jitsuroku) * Ten'an 1st year (857), October 15 - Granted the title "Yakushi Bosatsu Myōjin" (Nihon Montoku Tennō Jitsuroku) == Grounds == The carving of a squirrel and grapes on the front of the haiden is said to be the work of [[Hidari Jingorō]]. The guardian dogs (komainu) on either side of the second torii were made by a Showa period stone mason named Heikichi Iizuka. The path to the shrine is lined with camellia, tabunoki, and sudajii trees, forming a broadleaf forest that is designated a Natural Monument by Ibaraki Prefecture. The original shrine site is believed to be near the first torii, around the ruins of Hikantei.
